Washington, April 18. - No calamity since the
Galveston disaster has stirred the national
capital so deeply as did to-day's meagre tidings of
the San Francisco earthquake. At the White
House, in Congress, about the hotels and
throughout the business districts, no other
subject was discussed, and the extra editions of the
papers, which were frequently issued, were
cagerly bought and scanned for details.

Most of the members of the California delega~
tion in Congress were informed of the few facts
obtainable, alter they reached the Capitol, and
all expressed the utmost alarm for friends and
relatives in the stricken district. Practically
all the Congressmen immediately dispatched
messages of inquiry to those in whom they felt
a personal interest, but to a late hour to-night
none had been rewarded with an answer.

Representative Kahn, of California, was
almost prostrated by the news. Although his
wife is now living on Webster street, which the
A - -

reports indicate is well outside of the danger
zone, the Representative derives only little
comfort from this fact, for Mrs. Kahn gave birth to
a baby boy only the day before yesterday, and
her husband fears the effect upon her, in her
weakened condition, of the news of the
appalling calamity.

Senator Flint, whose home is in Los Angeles,
speaking of the fire at San Francisco, said:
"If they could only get water there would be
little doubt about getting the fire under
control. The town is built of red wood, and it takes
up water like a sponge.

"When water is thrown on a frame building,
and the home part of San Frencisco is bullt of
frame, the entire outer structure becomes
saturated, =o that it is proof against fire.

"But our waterworks in. San Francisco are
where they might readily be destroyed by such
a calemity &s this. They are on a high hill,
back of the town, and if the pipes leading to the
city have been badly broken so that they
cannot readily be repaired, the town is at the mercy
of the flames."

No communication could be effected with any
of ihe wireless stations within a hundred miles
of San Francisco, a fact which led the officials
here to believe that the zone of seismic
disturbance was more widespread than at first
believed.

Although no definite relief plans have thus far
been prepared, it is announced that the
government will render all possible ald to the sufferers.
The army, by means of tents, stored in the
warchouses of the quartermaster's department
in San Francisco, will be able to shelter in the
neighborhood of fifteen thousand and provide
scant protection with shelter tents for fully
twenty thousand more. The department has
now, at the depot there, 1,732 ordinary tents,
5 conical tents, with 50 more on the way, and
145 hospital tents that will accommodate six
persons each, and 323 wall tents.

Ample supplies for feeding many hundreds
of people are stored at the Presidio, the military
post on the outskirts of San Francisco, and if
these be found undamaged they will be placed
at the disposal of those who need them. The
National Red Cross is also making preparations
to engage in active relief work, and if later
advices confirm present reports, will dispatch
nurses, surgeons and supplies to the scene of the

Origin of San Francisco Disaster

scientific explanation of the earthquake at San
Francisco is given by Dr. G. F. Becker, chief of the

of seismological disturbances for the

Vesuvius. He ascribes the "shake" to an
unusually acute development in the process of

Pacific Coast for thousands of years. This
process consists in a readjustment of the rocks
forming the crust of the earth.

California is a chronic sufferer from
earthquakes in mild form, he says, but the severity
of the recent "shake" was due, in his opinion, to
the fact that there had been a suspension of the
shakes in recent years, and consequently the
disturbance was due to an accumulation, or. in
other words, a greater amount of earth was
shifted, or "faulted," in yesterday's "shake" than
| hae been the case before.

GREAT EARTHQUAKE LINE.
"It is a line characterized by a deep

earth.

Professor James F. Kemp, of Columbia
University, said vesterday that the probable cause
of the San Francisco earthquake was the
slipping along some fault" line - that is, a rift
where two geological deposits either of the same
or different periods meet in the interior of the
earth.

"The Pacific coast line is one of the latest
additions te the continent," said Professor Kemp,
"and because of this is far more subject to
selsmic disturbances than any other portion of the
country. Earthquakes are quite common, as is
shown by the records quoted in the Geological
Society's bulletins. According to these there
were DD such disturbances in California and
elsewhere along the Pacific coast in 1806, 80 ir
1897 and 24 in 1898, those being the latest
figures I hava.

"The worst shock felt in San Francisco prior
to the present one was on March 30, 1898. The
earthquake was felt mostly at the Mare Island
Navy Yard, Vallejo and Benicla. At the navy
vard the damage done was about £342,000."

It was pointed out to Professor Kemp that
San Francisco is along the same parallel as
Vesuvius and two other places in which seismic
disturbances have recently occurred, the
Ciscaucasian region and the Canary Islands. While this
was an interesting coincidence, Professor Kemp
said he thought there was no connection between
the three. In fact, Professor Kemp was
emphatically of the opinion that the earthquake
had nothing whatever to do with the recent
eruption at Mount Vesuvius or with veolcances
anywhere.

"The outer crust of the earth adjusts itself
from time to time," he said, "and this is most
probably one of those instances. Scientists do
not yet fully understand the exact nature of this
adjustment, but there are two suggestions as to
the probable cause which are generally accepted
- first, that on account of the radiation of heat
from the earth its interior is shrinking and
earthquake is the natural way the surface
adjusts itsel? to the new conditions; second, that
the earth is gradually slowing up in its rotation,
that it is flattening at the poles and swelling at
the equator, and that this causes the interior
slippings.

"The disturbance is unlikely to travel
eastward," Professor Kemp said.
"Seismic disturbances follow the direction of
the mountain ranges of a country, and in
Amer{ca this is generally north and south. The lines
of extreme weakness are always parallel with
the coast line of continents," he said.

"The Pacific coast line was formed by a giant
upheaval in prehistoric times, and beach lines
can still be seen far from the sea, showing that
the water was much higher at one time than it
is now. No change in the coast line has taken
place in recent years, except in Alaska, where,
in the neighborhood of the Muir Glacier, five

years ago, the line of the continent was raised.
~ Within the last century there was a change in

FORCED TO VACATE.

SAN FRANCISCO, April 18.?
At 1 :30 p.m. occupants of the
Western Union building, at Pine
and Montgomery streets, in which
Is located the Associated Press
office, were notified to move out. The
fire department was about to blow
up the adjoining buildings to stop
the progress of the fire.
CHICAGO, April
18.?Information received from San Francisco by
the mail division of the Union
Pacific railroad is to the effect that the
fire had swept from the water front
out as far as 9th street, a distance
of two miles. According to the
latest information, the buildings of
the Call, Examiner and Chronicle
were destroyed by fire. The
Merchants' Exchange, owned by the
Union Pacific railroad, was so badly
wrecked that nobody could enter it.

2 .15 p.m.?Reports from San Jose

Francisco situation is becoming
desperate. Fire still raging
furiously in all quarters of the city.
Postal telegraph office likely to go
any minute. It is impossible to
estimate the number of deaths, but it
is believed to exceed 300.

RECORDED IN VIENNA.

VIENNA, April 18.?A telegram
from the government observatory at
Laibach says that from 2125 to 2.59
o'clock this afternoon the

of great force and destructiveness.

disturbances were much more violent

hours six minutes, it follows that
the disturbance shown by the
seismograph at Laibach practically
synchronized with the first earthquake
shock experienced at San Francisco
at 5:13 a.m.

dis

SAN FRANCISCO, April 14.?

A. W. Hussey came to the station at
the hall of justice this morning and
told how, at the direction of a
policeman whom he did not know, but
whose star number he gave as 615,
he had cut the arteries in the wrists

the St. Katherine Hotel. According
to the statement made by Hussey,
the man was begging to be killed,
and the policeman shot at him, but
his aim was defective and the bullet
went wide of the mark. The officer
then handed Hussey a knife with
instructions to cut the veins in the
suffering man's wrists, and Hussey
obeyed orders.

Chief of Police Dinan directed
that Hussey be locked up. There
has been no opportunity to

believe that the awful calamity
rendered him insane,-and that the
incident reported to them had no
ex

bay have completely collapsed.

bay, carrying with them thousands
of tons of coal. The long wharf
was one of the most important
shipping points about the bay, aivl
freight traffic will be interrupted
greatly.

Speed of the California Earthquake.
A report of the velocity with which
Wednesday's San Francisco earth
tremors traveled from the Pacific to
the Atlantic coast has just been
issued by the coast and geodetic survey,
and strikingly illustrates the intensity
of the seismic storm. The preliminary
tremors, which consisted of small
irregular vibrations, are found by a
study of the seismograph records to
have been propagated across the
continent at an average rate of five and
a half miles per second. But the
motion of the most powerful and
destructive shock was too large to be
properly recorded by the seismograph.

These data indicate that all the
earth waves recorded on Wednesday
attained an exceptionally high speed.
The rate of propagation in the great
Charleston earthquake of 1886, as
computed front the time data, was 775
feet per second. In the terrible
Japanese earthquake of October, 1891,
the computed average velocity did'
not exceed 1.3 miles per second. But
in the Zante earthquake of March 20.
1893, the velocity was very nearly five
miles. - New York Herakl.

SAN FRANCISCO EARTHQUAKE
Greatest Catastrophe the Country Has Ever Known Beggars
Description - Immediately Followed by Fire, and Today Only
OneFourth of the Golden Gate City Stands as Monument to the
Disaster - The Entire Country Stunned by News From Scene.

San Franciaco. - San Francisco is
the city desolate. Earthquake and fire
have almost entirely destroyed the
Metropolis of the Golden West and
famine and destitution adds to the
horror of the death roll.
At 5:15 o'clock, April 18th., an
earthquake shook the whole city and
surrounding country. One shock
apparently lasted two minutes and there
•was almost immediate collapse of
flimsy structures all over the city. The
•water supply was cut off and when
fire boke out in the various sections
there was nothing to do but let it
burn. Telegraphic and telephonic
communication was shut off, the
Western Union being one of the first
buildings to be destroyed. Electric
power was shut off and railroads and
tferrv boats suspended operations.

The earthquake came without any
•warning, its motion apparently being
from east to west. At first the
upheaval of the earth was gradual, but
in a few seconds it increased in
intensity. Chimneys began to fall and
holdings to crack, tottering on their
foundations. People became panic
stricken and rushed into the streets
most of them in their night attire.
They were met by showers of falling
buildings, bricks, cornices and walls.
Many were instantly crushed to death
while others were deradfully mangled.
Those who remained indoors generally
escaped with their lives, though scores
were struck by detached plaster,
pictures and articles thrown to the floor
by the shock.

The tall steel frame structures stood
the strain better than brick buildings,
few of them being 'badly damaged.
The big eleven story Monadnock build
ing is course of construction,
adjoining the Palace hotel, was an
exception, however, its rear walls
collapsing and many cracks being mac*:
across its front.
'Some of the docks and freight
sheds along the water front slid into
the bay. Deep fiissures opened in the
tilled in ground near the shore, and
the Union ferry depot was irreparably
injured. Its high tower still stands,
bat will have to be torn down.

A portion 0f the new city hall,
which cost more than $7,000,000
collapsed, the roof sliding into the court
yard and the' smaller towers
tumbling down with the great dome being
moved but not falling.
The postoffice, one of the finest in
the United States, was badly
shattered.
The Valencia Hotel a four-story
wooden building, sank into the
basement, a pile of splintered timbers,
under which were pinned many dead
end dying occupants of the house.
The basement was full of water, and
some of the helpless victims were
•drowned.

Scarcely had the earth ceased to
shake when fires broke out
simultaneously in many places. The fire
department promptly responded to the
(first calls for aid, but it was found
that the water mains had been
rendered useless by the underground
movement. Fanned by a light breeze
the flames quickly spread and soon
many blocks were doomed. Then
dynamiting was resorted to, and the
sound of frequent explosions added to
the terror of the people.

All efforts to stay the fire,
however, proved futile. The south side of
Market street, from Ninth street to
the bay was soon ablaze, the fire
covering a belt two blocks wide. On this
the main thoroughfare of the city,
•was located many of the finest
edifices in the city, including the Grant,
Parrott, Flood, Call, Examiner and
Monadnoek buildings, the Palace and
Grand hotels, and numerous wholesale
houses.
At the same time the commercial
establishments and banks -north -of
Market street were burning. The
burning district in this section
extended from Sansome street to the water
front, and from Market street to the
bay. Fires also broke out in the
Mission, and the entire city was soop in
flames.

President Roosevelt, after a
consultation with Miss Mabel Boardman of
the American Red Cross, issued an
appeal to the American people to aid
San Francisco. He asked that all
contributions be made through the
American National Red Cross, who have
effected systematic arrangements to
distribute needed assistance. The full
text of the president's proclamation
follows:
"In the face of so terrible and
appalling a national calamity as that
which lias befallen San Francisco, the
outpouring of the nation's aid should
as far as possible be entrusted to the
American Red Cross, the national
organization best fitted to undertake the
work. A specially appointed agent,
Dr. Edward Divine, starts today from
New York for California, to
co-operate there with the Red Cross branch
in the relief work. In order that this
work may he well systematized and

and in order that the contributions
that I am sure will flow in with
lavish generosity, may be wisely
administered, I appeal to the people of the
United States, to all cities, chambers
of commerce, boards of trade, relief
committees and individuals to express
their sympathy and render their aid
by contributions to the American
National Red Cross.
"They can be sent to 'Hon. Charles
Hallam Keep, Red Cross Treasurer,
Washington, D. C., Mr. Jacob H.
Schiff, New York, Red Cross treasurer
or other local Red Cross treasurers
to be forwarded by telegraph from
Washington to the Red Cross agents
and officers in California.

(Signed) THEO. ROOSEVELT."

OAKLAND HELPS ALL
OVER 75,000 REIUGEES FROM
FRISCO RECEIVE SHELTER.
Free Transportation for Those Who
Want to Leave - No One Goes
Hungry - Destitute Being Cared for -
Wedding Occurs; Groom Had $1.30
- Chinese Fared Worst of All.
Oakland is caring for 75,000 people
rendered homeless by the disaster, and
is prepared (o care for twice as many.
The height of the influx has been
leached and the number of refugees is
slightly decreasing. Although they are
still coming in large numbers, more
are leaving on every train for various
points. Requests for free
transportation are investigated as closely as
possible, and all the deserving are sent
away. Women and children and
married men who wish to join their
families in various parts of the state are
given the preference. The
transportation bureau is on a street corner,
where a man stands on a box and calls

the names of those who are entitled
to passes. No one now goes hungry
here and few lack shelter, but cots
and bedding are needed. At the First
Presbyterian church 1800 were feil
Sunday night and 1000 people will
sleep there tonight. Pews have been
turned into beds. Cots are in the
aisles, in the gallery and in the
Sunday school room. Every available inch
of space is occupied by some
substitute for a bed.
A Rockefeller Camp.
John D. Rockefeller has sent money
for the establishment of a new camp,
which will bear his name. Los Angeles
has provided for a camp to
accommodate 1000 people, and has sent 60
physicians and nurses to look after
the sick in it. Food is also coming in
from that city, and more help if
needfront that city.

An important piece of work that is
going on at relief headquarters in the
chamber of commerce rooms is the
registration of refugees. There are 45
clerks engaged in this work alone. All
v ho register are catalogued by cards,
which bear their names and old and
new addresses. In this manner dozens
of families have been reunited and
friends have found each other. A line
of anxious inquirers extends far out
into the street, while others file past
to register or leave an inquiry for
some one who might seek them. There
is an employment bureau, where work
is provided whenever possible.
Hundreds of letters pout in. and the
information is given whenever
possible.

Fraternal Societies Busy.
Independent of I he regular relief
committee, much work is being done
by fraternal societies, the members of
which meet all incoming trains and
take care of the destitute. ^
A wedding took place at the relief
bureau at midnight last night.
Despite the fact that the groom had
only $1.30, the newly married couple
looked cheerfully on the prospect that
confronted them and departed happy
and hopeful.
Relief for Actors.
A relief bureau especially for
theatrical people is situated on Broadway,
near Twelfth, and transportation east
has been furnished 200 people. One
hundred are being taken care of at the
Bell theater, and will be given tickets
out of town as soon as possible. Stars,
as well as music hall singers, are
welcomed at the bureau, and many of
them looked hungry for a sight of the

lights of Broadway.
Chinese in Sad Plight.
The Chinese fared worst of all of
the San Francisco refugees. Some got
out with their belongings at the first
alarm of fire, but others remained
until the afternoon. Then, as the flames
came closer, they were driven out by
the soldiers without being allowed to
get food or clothing. A hasty guard
shot one as he was going into his
stcre for goods. Nearly 10,000 of them
have arrived here, and the majority
have been cared for in the local
Chinatown. Nearly all of them are
absolute'y destitute.

FRISCO MAILS ARE OPEN NOW.
Only 50 Bags Destroyed by the Fire
and Earthquake.
At a meeting of the postal
authorities with the military, held at the
jostoffice building, plans have been
completed for the resumption of mail
service. The San Francisco
postoffice is in full operation. Three
hundred and fifty men are at work in the
main office at Seventh and Mission
streets.
Inspection by Lieutenant George R.
Ärmst rung and Postoffice Inspector
O'Connell show that all but 50 bags of
mail which went through the fire have
been recovered, and now mail is
being handled expeditiously. All trains
are carrying mails into the city and
this is being distributed at the
postoffice. which was only partially
damaged. Branch offices under the
coauthority of the postmaster and the
military, are being established
throughout the city and the adjacent
hills, where the refugees are camped.

All mail matter should be addressed
to the old street number in San
Francisco unless the new address is
positively known. Nine branch offices are
in operation. Money orders are being
cashed as rapidly as funds can be
secured. The postmaster is completing
arrangements with the
superintendent of the mint to convert into
cash the paper now on hand in the
postoffice. All money orders will
be paid on demand, and represent the
only possible means of sending money
into San Francisco at present. No
banks are open, nor will they be for
2u to 30 days. Letters are being
accepted without stamps or envelopes
and will reach their destination
without delay.

The people of San Francisco,
particularly the men of large property
and affairs, are thinking only of the
future. There is a spirit of
resignation among all classes and a
déterminai ion on the part of those who
have suffered the most from the
great fire to rebuild. In truth
"rebuild" is the watchword everywhere.

COAL MINE HORROR
TWENTY-TWO KILLED BY DUST
EXPLOSION IN COLORADO.

Forty Miles West of
Trinidad - Seventeen Miners, Who Were Working
3700 Feet From Entrance Escaped -
Most of the Dead Are Italians and
Japanese.
As the result of a dust explosion in
a mine of the Colorado Fuel & Iron
company, 40 miles west of Trinidad,
Colo., shortly before noon Sunday, 22
miners are known to be dead and
one other is missing, with little hope
of being found alive.
There were 40 men in the mine at
the time of the explosion. Seventeen
miners, who were working 3700 feet
from the entrance, escaped unhurt
through another opening.

The explosion occurred in rooms 3
and 4 near the main entrance, and
was the result of a windy shot, which
ignited the dust.
An order for 22 coffins has been
received by a local undertaker here,
that many bodies having been taken
out today. The mine was not badly
damaged, and work can be resumed in
a couple of days. The mine employed
180 men.
Miners from adjacent camps are
assisting in the rescue. Superintendent
Robert O'Neil left here on a special
train at noon, and is personally
directing the rescue work.

Among the dead is James Reed, fire
l oss. Most of the others qre Italians
and Japanese.

unique feature in the military history
of the country.
It Is the first time a government
expedition has sailed to a foreign shore,
formed a gay military pageant and
marched through the streets of the
second city of that foreign land to erect
monuments to its victories on fields
over which its ting no longer flies. That
tills was possible in Cuba Is due to
tlie peculiar situation that resulted
when the United States kept the sacred
promises made when war was declared.

Spain, the vanquished, was driven out,
and the fairest land In the West
Indies turned over to a native republic.
The chief ceremony which the
expedition conducted was the dedication of
a simple, dignified, substantial battle
monument on the ruing of Fort el Vlso,
near the little town of El Caney, five
miles back in the green-clad Cuban hills
from Santiago. The official party from
tlie Sumner Included four generals,
two admirals, four colonels, four
lieutenant colonels, seven majors and five
captains. From tlie United States
cruiser Y'ankee came three companies
of marines and a battalion of sailors.

The Cuban republic was represented by
Gen. Andrade, secretary of the Interior,
escorted by three companies of
Cuban const artillery and a company of
Infantry. It was an impressive service.

The Course of the Flames.
Everything worth mentioning except this
residence district was burned over or on
fire this afternoon. The flames finished
with the business district, ran south
through what remained of the tenement

region, a region of cheap residences, and

All hope of saving any considerable part

throughout the entire magnificent residence
and financial quarters by the swift work
of thirty-five hours, and with a black ruin
covering more than seven square miles cut
Into her very heart, the city now waits In
a stupor the inevitable reign of starvation
and of the very possible anarchy that must

But the seismograph would de
absolutely useless {f there were not
mechanical devices to properly record
the wave motions. The drum on
which the prepared paper is wound
is turned by clockwork. It makes
a complete revolution every hour.
When there are no shocks the

soot-covered paper. 1 e the drum

describe a lateral motion in order that
the needle may not retracé the same
line time and again, and thus
prevent the department from knowing
at just what hour a disturbance
takes place.

There is still another attachment
which enables the Weather Bureau
to determine not only during what
hour any particular disturbance
occurs, but the exact minute and
second. There is an electric clock in
connection with the needle which
causes the point of the needle to
make a very slight fluctuation every
minute. These fluctuations are
recorded on the coated paper as slight
niches breaking the uniformity of
the line.

One curious phase of the present opera

the audiences, For several years a good
many mutes have been attending
performances of panoramas, spectacular
plays and highly spiced melodramas; but

sight; consequently they choose seats

SPEED WILL BE DISASTROUS
Geologists Say Neighboring Rivers Are
Making Region Lopsided and
Shake-Up Possible.
Washington may experience an
earthquake some day. according to N. H.
Darton, of the Geological Survey, who
nas made an extensive [nvestigation of
the geology of the District of Columbia.
There have been extensive movements
in the past and there is amvle evidence
to show that the land here is sinking,
though at a very low rate, probably not
over one foot a century. A gradual
movement of the land causes no
damage, but an eathquake results when a
sudden upward or downward movement
takes place, even f the vertical
displacement is very small

A few years ago there was visible, in
the railroad cut just east of Rock Creek
bridge on Cincinnati street, a fault or
break in the strata, indicating a drop
of about two fee. This happened since
the glacial epoch, and probably was
attended by a great earthquake, but was
lonz before Washington was inhabited.
Movements of this character may
recur, as in the case of the Charleston
earthquake a few years ago.

A vast amount of detritus is washed
from the mountains and slopes to the
west and carried by such rivers as the
Potomac, James, and Susquehanna to
the ocean. There is a gradual
diminution of matter on the west and
aceumulation of weight to the east. This
disturbs the equillbrium and causes
subsidence of the land. it Is to be ex
pected that the readjustment will be so
gradual that no serious disturbances
vill follow, but there are some
possibilii es that at a remote time the results
risy be gatastrophic.

"The first question to be asked is of
astronomers, for it is generally believed
that earthquakes are to a large extent
caused by the failure of the earth to
swing perfectly true. Sometimes it
gets a little bit off its course and the
reaction in swinging back to its true
position involves a tremendous strain
on the center. This is said to be so
great that it results in twisting or
breaking earth's crust. Therefore, to

find the present disturbance you must
get astronomers to tell you if they have
noticed any deviation in the earth's
axis within the past few days. The
recent eruption of Vesuvius is probably
due to the same cause."

Prof. Tarr Tells of Changing Physical
Conditions on Pacific Coast.

New York, April 19.The Times
today prints a statement from Ralph
Stockman Tarr, professor of dynamatic
geology and physical geography at
Cornell university on the subject of the
San Francisco earthquake. Professor
Tarr was formerly connected with the
United States geological survey and the
Smithsonian institute at Washington.
He is considered an authority on seismic
disturbances. He says:
"It is too early to pronounce a final
opinion upon nature and cause of the
San Francisco earthquake, but from
what has been said it will be seen that
it is probable that this shock is the
result of movements along one or more
fault lines in the course of the natural
growth of the coast ranges, which
geologists have long known to be still in
progress thruout the entire extent of
California. That the coast ranges are
growing is proved by numerous
evidences. There are upraised shore lines

at various points along the California
coast, proving recent uplift. The very
bay of San Francisco is the result of a
geologically recent subsidence of this
part of the coast which has admitted
the sea into the gorge that the
Sacramento river formerly cut across the
coast ranges. This forms the Golden
Gate and in the broader mountain
valley behind the sea has spread out to
form the bay.
"Whether the center of greatest
disturbance of the present shock is in or
near the city cannot yet be told, tho
the meager reports so far received
indicate this. If it is, San Francisco is in
danger of future disasters."

of estimated losses to be followed at a later
date, within a reasonable time, by a sworn
statement. The results of these statements were
given to the press, and the pamphlets
containing such results were sent to all inquirers. Soms
such procedure will be followed in the case of
the California conflagrations.

New York representatives of several of the
large fire insurance companies consulted
together yesterday and will have more
consultations to-day regarding tha settlement of fire
losses in San Francisco. It seemed to be the
opinion that the companies would have to deal
broadly with San Francisco sufferers, although
the companies would not have to pay losses in
buildings which were thrown down by the
earthquake before they took fire.

It was said by representatives of some of the
companies that quibbling on the subject would
not pay, and that in case of doubt it would be
for the interest of the companies to pay losses.
The condition of the ruins will tell in the bulk
of the cases, and testimony will be abundant to
show which buildings were left standing intact
after the earthquake and were subsequently
destroyed by fire.

Representatives of the insurance companies
expressed bellef that the total losses by fire in
San Francisco would not exceed F150,000,000.
Some of the American companies might be
crippled seriously in paying the losses, it was said,
but there was no fear that the losses would not
be paid. As to the foreign companies, it was said
they probably would draw on their home
resources to pay the losses, leaving the American
balances undisturbed. .

The Liverpool and London and Globe
Insurance Company announced yesterday that {ts
san Francisco losses would be paid immediately
on adjustment, and that its United States assets,
in accordance with precedent, would not be

drawn upon. The company's losses in San
Francisco may reach $4,000,000.
The North British and Mercantile Fire
Insurance Company has cabled its New York
representatives to pay losses sustained in the San
Francisco disaster as soon as they are adjusted.
The company has outstanding insurance in San
Francisco to the amount of $3,560,000.

It was announced by Philemon L. Hoadley,
vice-president of the American Fire Insurance
Company, in Newark yesterday that his
company may lose about $1,000,000 as a result of
the earthquake and fire in San Francisco. Word
was received from Oakland from H. F. Gordon,
a general manager for the company, yesterday
afternoon which said that all the business
buildings had been burned and that practically all
but the agents' accounts had been lost. Mr.
Hoadley declared, however, that whatever may
be the loss the company is ready and will adjust
all claims promptly after an investigation of the
ruins has been made.

It was ascertained yesterday that the
insurance brokers in this city were not withdrawing
{insurance from any company to an extent
indicating belief in the company's insolvency. It
was said that the brokers had agreed not to give
new business to a few of the companies until the
extent of the San Francisco losses of those
companies had been ascertained.

"The Pacific Coast Review" says that 105
insurance companies underwrote fire risks in San
Francisco and carried a total of $250,000,000 on
buildings and contents. The total assessed value
of the buildings of the city was $128,000,000. On
account of its low fire loss for many years, San
Francisco was a favorite with the insurance
companies. Over one-half of the total risks, it
is sald, were carried by foreign insurance
companies and it is stated that yesterday's break
of 70 points in sterling was due to British and
other forelgn companies selling in preparation for
the remittance of many millions of dollars of loss
clalms that must come here. The effect of the
payment of fire losses on a large scale by
foreign insurance companies will be the accumula~
tion here of a great quantity of funds, for these
claims will be paid long before the funds are

required for rebuilding. The total reconstruction
of the city will take probably not less than
seven or eight years.

have lost their lives. The only person connected
